body:
Why alternatives to conventional batteries are useful

Battery storage and pumped-storage hydropower are important technologies, but they are not suitable for every situation. Some applications need very rapid bursts of power, some need large quantities of energy for many hours, and others require heat rather than electricity.

Alternative storage technologies differ mainly in what physical form of energy they store and how they release that energy.

Mechanical energy storage

Flywheel energy storage

A flywheel stores energy in a rotating mass. Electricity drives a motor that accelerates the flywheel. When electricity is needed, the rotating mass slows and drives an electrical generator.

The stored energy is rotational kinetic energy. Flywheels can respond rapidly and are useful for short-duration power support and frequent cycling. However, they generally are not the preferred method for storing very large quantities of electricity over several days because of their energy capacity and continuing losses.

Compressed-air energy storage

Compressed-air energy storage (CAES) uses electricity to compress air and store it at high pressure. Later, the stored air is released and expanded to help drive a turbine or other machinery that produces electricity.

Large-scale systems may use suitable underground geological formations, such as salt caverns, although other storage arrangements are possible. This creates an important geographical distinction: the availability of a suitable underground storage site can influence where a large CAES project is practical.

Compression raises the temperature of air, while expansion cools it. Different CAES designs manage heat differently, including systems that store heat produced during compression. Therefore, compressed-air storage involves both mechanical and thermal considerations even though it is commonly grouped under mechanical storage.

Thermal energy storage

Thermal energy storage (TES) retains energy in the form of heat or cold. The energy may later be used directly for heating or cooling, or it may be converted into electricity.

Molten-salt storage

In some concentrating solar-thermal power (CSP) plants, mirrors concentrate sunlight to produce high-temperature heat. Molten salts can retain that heat in insulated tanks. The stored heat can later be used to generate steam or otherwise drive a power-conversion process to produce electricity.

The molten salt stores thermal energy. It is not an electrochemical battery, and it does not directly store electrons.

Ice, chilled water and other thermal materials

Water, ice, rocks and other materials can also store thermal energy. An ice-storage system can make ice when cooling demand or electricity-system stress is lower and use that stored cooling later. In such an arrangement, storage may reduce future electricity demand without generating electricity itself.

Thermal storage used for heating or cooling is not necessarily an electricity-to-electricity storage system. The final useful output may be heat or cooling rather than electrical energy.

Chemical energy storage using hydrogen

Electricity can produce hydrogen through electrolysis, in which electrical energy drives the splitting of water into hydrogen and oxygen. Hydrogen can then be stored as a chemical energy carrier.

Stored hydrogen may later be used as fuel or converted back into electricity through a fuel cell or suitable generating equipment. Hydrogen storage may be considered for long-duration applications because the hydrogen can potentially be held for extended periods in appropriate storage facilities.

However, converting electricity to hydrogen and then back into electricity involves several stages and energy losses. Its electricity-to-electricity efficiency is generally lower than that of direct lithium-ion battery storage. Storage, transport, infrastructure and safety requirements also affect its suitability.

Comparing the main alternatives

TechnologyStored formCommon applicationImportant condition
FlywheelRotational kinetic energyVery rapid, short-duration power supportRotating machinery and continuing losses
Compressed airEnergy associated with compressed gasMulti-hour electricity storageSuitable pressure-storage system and heat management
Molten saltHeatDelayed generation in solar-thermal plantsHeat storage and later thermal conversion
Ice or chilled waterStored coolingShifting building cooling demandUseful output may be cooling, not electricity
HydrogenChemical energyPotential long-duration or fuel applicationsConversion losses and storage infrastructure
Redox flow batteryElectrochemical energyMulti-hour stationary electricity storageExternal electrolyte tanks and circulation

These application descriptions are typical uses, not fixed discharge-duration limits. Plant size and design can change how long a technology operates.

A brief distinction: supercapacitors

Supercapacitors store energy mainly through electrical charge separation rather than the bulk chemical reactions used by conventional batteries. They can charge and discharge rapidly and are well suited to brief power demands. They generally store much less energy per unit mass than lithium-ion batteries, making them different from long-duration energy storage systems.

Prelims focus

  • Flywheels store rotational kinetic energy.
  • CAES stores energy through compressed air.
  • Molten-salt storage retains heat and is associated with CSP applications.
  • Hydrogen produced by electrolysis stores chemical energy.
  • Ice storage can shift cooling demand without generating electricity.
  • Trap: Every energy storage technology does not necessarily deliver electricity as its final output.

[U.S. Department of Energy, Solar Integration: Solar Energy and Storage Basics, sections on mechanical, electrochemical and thermal storage; U.S. Department of Energy, Solar Thermal Energy Storage and Heat Transfer Media, section What Are Thermal Energy Storage and Heat Transfer Media?; U.S. Department of Energy, Pumped Storage Hydropower: Technology Strategy Assessment, July 2023, introduction to storage classifications; U.S. Department of Energy, Lithium-ion Batteries: Technology Strategy Assessment, July 2023, Storage Innovations 2030 technology-family list; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Other Storage Technologies: Mechanical, Thermal and Chemical Methods

body:
Electricity grids need both rapid response and sustained energy

Electricity storage is valuable because it can change when power is absorbed from or supplied to the grid. Different grid problems require different combinations of response speed, power rating and energy capacity.

A short disturbance may require a rapid change in power for only seconds. Evening electricity demand may require several hours of sustained generation. A prolonged period of low renewable output may require still more stored energy or additional sources of firm supply.

Energy shifting

Energy shifting means charging storage during one period and discharging during another. It is especially useful when solar or wind generation is plentiful at a time that does not coincide with maximum electricity demand.

For example, midday solar energy can charge batteries that discharge during an evening demand peak. Pumped storage can serve a similar purpose by pumping water uphill during a surplus period and generating later.

Peak shaving and renewable-energy integration

Peak shaving means reducing the highest demand placed on a system or network by supplying some of that demand from storage. A battery may also reduce the peak power taken by a commercial facility from the grid.

Renewable-energy integration includes absorbing some surplus generation, reducing the need to curtail available renewable output, and supplying stored energy when renewable generation falls. Storage does not eliminate all variability; it helps manage that variability within the limits of its capacity.

Firming or smoothing renewable output means reducing sudden variations in delivered power or maintaining a more predictable delivery profile for an intended period. Achieving firm supply continuously requires sufficient energy, suitable controls and, where necessary, additional generation.

Frequency response, reserves and reliability

The grid must maintain a close balance between total generation and consumption. When an imbalance occurs, system frequency can move away from its target. Suitable storage systems can quickly increase electricity delivery or reduce electricity absorption to help restore balance.

Frequency regulation involves responding to smaller continuing imbalances. Operating reserves are resources kept available to respond to larger disturbances or unexpected losses of supply. Storage may provide these services if it has suitable controls, sufficient available power and the necessary stored energy.

A battery that responds in a fraction of a second may be valuable for frequency support. But the same battery cannot sustain full output after its usable stored energy is exhausted.

Black start and backup power

Black start is the capability to begin restoring an electricity system after a major outage without relying on an already energised external grid. Some suitably equipped storage installations can contribute to black-start arrangements, but this is not an automatic capability of every battery or pumped-storage plant.

Backup power likewise requires more than stored energy. The installation must have appropriate controls, isolation and connections to supply the intended loads safely.

Matching a service to a technology

Grid requirementImportant characteristicSuitable technology examples
Very rapid power correctionFast response; relatively little total energy may sufficeBattery, flywheel or supercapacitor
Short backup or demand smoothingFast response and adequate short-duration capacityBattery
Evening peak supplySeveral hours of usable energyBattery, pumped storage or suitable flow battery
Large multi-hour energy shiftingSubstantial energy capacityPumped storage, battery or suitable compressed-air system
Potential extended storageAbility to retain and release energy over long periodsAppropriately designed chemical or other long-duration storage

The table identifies possible matches rather than exclusive assignments. Actual suitability depends on project design, the cost and availability of the stored energy, local conditions and the performance required by the grid.

Why storage technologies are complementary

One storage technology does not have to perform every grid service. A power system may use batteries for very fast responses, pumped storage for substantial evening demand, and other technologies where long-duration energy or thermal storage is more suitable.

India's Ministry of Power recognised multiple electricity-system uses for storage in its National Framework for Promoting Energy Storage Systems, August 2023. These include renewable-energy integration, peak management and grid-support services. The framework is a policy document dated August 2023; its forecasts should not be treated as measurements of storage already installed in 2026.

Prelims focus

  • Energy shifting transfers electricity use between time periods.
  • Peak shaving reduces the highest demand seen by a system or network.
  • Frequency regulation helps correct short-term generation-demand imbalances.
  • Black start requires the capability to restore supply without an already energised external grid.
  • Storage suitability depends on response speed, power rating and usable energy capacity.
  • Trap: Fast response does not imply long discharge duration.

[Ministry of Power, Government of India, National Framework for Promoting Energy Storage Systems, August 2023, Section 4, Applications and Use Cases of ESS in Power Sector, pp. 3–4; U.S. Department of Energy, Battery Energy Storage Systems: Considerations for Implementation, 5 August 2025, slides 13–15, energy shifting, peak shaving and grid services; U.S. Department of Energy, Pumped Storage Hydropower, section Grid Reliability, Resilience, and Integration; sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Grid Services and Choosing Storage by Required Duration

body:
Geography determines which storage technologies fit a location

Energy storage is not distributed solely according to where electricity is generated. The most suitable storage technology also depends on the physical conditions required for storing energy.

Pumped-storage hydropower requires a useful difference in elevation between reservoirs, suitable land and water arrangements, and a connection to the electricity system. Hilly or mountainous areas may provide favourable height differences, but terrain alone does not establish whether a project is feasible.

Grid batteries have fewer requirements for natural elevation or water reservoirs. They can be located near electricity demand, renewable-energy plants or substations, subject to land, safety, environmental and grid-connection requirements.

Compressed-air storage may benefit from suitable underground formations where large quantities of pressurised air can be held. Hydrogen storage also depends on appropriate storage infrastructure and, for some large-scale options, geological conditions. Molten-salt thermal storage can be especially useful in concentrating solar-thermal installations, which depend on suitable solar resources.

Examples of pumped-storage projects in India

The following examples identify locations and installed or listed capacities. They also distinguish project classification from verified pumping operation.

ProjectStateCapacity and relevant fact
Tehri Pumped Storage PlantUttarakhand1000 MW; 4 units of 250 MW each, all commercially operational by 12 April 2026
Purulia Pumped Storage ProjectWest Bengal900 MW; listed by CEA as an operating off-stream, closed-loop project
Pinnapuram Pumped Storage ProjectAndhra Pradesh1680 MW; listed by CEA as an operating off-stream, closed-loop project in its 2026 status sheet
KadanaGujarat240 MW; listed in CEA project tables, but its pumping mode was reported non-operational at the end of 2025
Sardar Sarovar River Bed Power HouseGujarat1200 MW; listed in CEA project tables, but its pumping mode was reported non-operational at the end of 2025

Tehri: an example of operating pumped storage

The Tehri Pumped Storage Plant is situated in Tehri Garhwal, Uttarakhand. It uses the Tehri Dam reservoir as its upper reservoir and the Koteshwar Dam reservoir as its lower reservoir.

It has 4 units of 250 MW each, giving a total capacity of 1000 MW. According to THDC India Limited, its units entered commercial operation on 7 June 2025, 10 July 2025, 12 December 2025 and 12 April 2026, respectively.

THDC's project information identifies a round-trip efficiency of more than 75%. That figure refers to Tehri's stated project characteristics; it should not be assumed to be the efficiency of every pumped-storage plant.

Gujarat is among the beneficiary states identified for electricity from Tehri Pumped Storage Plant. Thus, a state may benefit from a storage project located outside its geographical boundaries through electricity-grid arrangements.

Gujarat's Kadana and Sardar Sarovar projects

Kadana is associated with the Mahi River system in Gujarat's Mahisagar district. The Central Electricity Authority lists it with 4 units of 60 MW, totalling 240 MW, under Gujarat State Electricity Corporation Limited.

Sardar Sarovar is associated with the Narmada River in Gujarat's Narmada district. Its River Bed Power House is listed with 6 units of 200 MW, totalling 1200 MW, under Sardar Sarovar Narmada Nigam Limited.

Installed capacity is not proof of pumping operation

In its January 2026 roadmap, using project-status information as of 31 December 2025, the Central Electricity Authority specifically stated that Kadana and Sardar Sarovar were not operational in pumping mode.

CEA's later 2026 project-status sheet continued to place both projects in its in-operation category, but that listing alone does not establish that pumping had become functional. The explicit non-operational statement relates to the 31 December 2025 reporting date; it must not be silently converted into a verified status for every later date.

The distinction matters because hydropower generation can be possible even where the equipment or operational arrangements needed for pumping are not functional. A project's generating capacity and its actually available pumped-storage capability are not always equivalent.

Understanding project status and official targets

An energy project may appear in official documents as a potential site, a proposed project, an approved project, a project under construction or a commissioned installation. These stages are different.

For pumped-storage projects, even the phrase in operation should be interpreted carefully where official reports separately qualify pumping functionality. A planned commissioning date is a target, not proof that commissioning has occurred.

India's Ministry of Power issued a National Framework for Promoting Energy Storage Systems in August 2023, while the Central Electricity Authority publishes project-status information and planning documents. These sources serve different purposes: one sets out a policy framework, while the other can identify specific plants and their reported stages of development.

One-glance classification of energy storage

The central distinction across the entire subtopic is the form in which energy is retained. Lithium-ion, sodium-ion, lead-acid and flow batteries use electrochemical reactions. Pumped storage uses the gravitational potential energy of elevated water. Flywheels store rotational kinetic energy. Compressed-air systems retain energy in pressurised gas. Thermal storage retains heat or cold. Hydrogen stores chemical energy that can later be used as fuel or converted into electricity.

Prelims focus

  • Tehri Pumped Storage Plant: Uttarakhand, 1000 MW, all 4 units commercially operational by 12 April 2026.
  • Purulia Pumped Storage Project: West Bengal, 900 MW.
  • Kadana: Gujarat, Mahisagar district, 240 MW.
  • Sardar Sarovar River Bed Power House: Gujarat, Narmada district, 1200 MW.
  • CEA's January 2026 roadmap reported Kadana and Sardar Sarovar non-operational in pumping mode as of 31 December 2025.
  • Trap: Project capacity, project listing and actual pumping capability are 3 different facts.

[Central Electricity Authority, Roadmap to 100 GW of Hydro Pumped Storage Projects by 2035–36, January 2026, Section 4.1, In-Operation Pumped Storage Projects, project status as of 31 December 2025, pp. 17–18; Central Electricity Authority, Category Wise Status of Pumped Storage Development in India, 2026 status sheet, Section A, PSP in Operation, including project, district and capacity entries, consulted 16 November 2026; THDC India Limited, Tehri Pumped Storage Plant (1000 MW), General Features and Operational Performance, project information updated in 2026, consulted 16 November 2026; Ministry of Power, National Framework for Promoting Energy Storage Systems, August 2023, Sections 4 and 5.6; U.S. Department of Energy, Pumped Storage Hydropower, site requirements and operating principles, consulted 16 November 2026.]
